extracted.intended_audience: Public Information Officers (PIOs) and emergency managers handling media relations during incidents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for Public Information Officers on interacting with media, writing press releases, conducting briefings and interviews, managing media access during incidents, and using social media and digital channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Each media outlet has a specific deadline; identify and meet them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a media log and record each media representative’s deadline in the first entry or ask reporters directly; provide requested information in time for them to meet their deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor information to the outlet's scope: national/regional want big picture; local want specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know who you are talking to so you can emphasize the most important items appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire Service Protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact wire services first for incidents with significant potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire reporters usually want large amounts of detailed information, may request sidebars/features, and may visit the site; local reporters may sell stories to wire services; some outlets publish wire copy verbatim while others re-report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper reporters want detailed information, human-interest angles, and visuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide suggestions for human interest or sidebar stories, graphics, and photographs; treat photographers like reporters; coordinate photographic access with the Operations Section Chief to determine best photo locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio is immediate and requires frequent, concise updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide frequent updates, especially during drive times; stories are very short (2–3 sentences); be prepared for taped telephone interviews (they will notify before taping) and for live or call-in talk shows that can last from minutes to an hour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television Interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Television prioritizes pictures and human emotion; wants quick, general information and visuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide photos/video quickly; be prepared for on-set or live interviews; satellite coverage can enable 24/7 live broadcasting from remote locations—plan accordingly for visuals and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web/Digital Media Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Web/digital channels are increasingly primary news sources and must be accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide MPEG audio/video, GIS/real-time GIS, and satellite overlays when appropriate; recognize that TV, radio, and newspapers use websites to gather information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Media Use and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media offers two-way communication and situational awareness but presents challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social platforms to share updates and receive geo-data, text, pictures, and video; be mindful of verification, public expectations, and the need to manage misinformation and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIO–Media Relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce tension by pre-planning and understanding media needs and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper PIO performance, preparation, and a clear understanding of media practices lessen incident managers' pressure from media presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Coordination with Incident Commander
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet early with the Incident Commander to agree media operating procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss expectations for media coverage, availability of Incident Commander and personnel for interviews, approval process for releasing information, policy on flying in agency/contracted aircraft, and how much access will be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Access Options
rubrics_metrics.description: Incident managers can provide open access, deny access, or control access—each has consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing open access is best for ensuring accurate sourcing. Denying access is usually counter-productive because others will speak. Controlled access is tempting but often creates hard feelings and operational cost; plan to have enough PIOs or escorts to guide media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing Information and Interviews (PIO Task)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be proactive in providing information and interviews to reduce demands on incident personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not wait for media to come; go to them when you have information to share to avoid misinterpretation and to preserve operational staff time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Briefings — Scheduling and Format
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedule briefings to save time and help media plan; set time, location, and duration to media needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good times: generally 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m.; location should be accessible without interfering with incident management; keep briefings short (e.g., 15 minutes of information then Q&A); notify media of time/place and include all interested organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Briefings — Preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare speakers and visual aids to ensure effective briefings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help Incident Commander and representatives with talking points and likely questions; prepare and post maps, charts, status boards; develop/distribute handouts containing the same information; PIO should start the briefing, set rules, make introductions, and conclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Briefing Content Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include what the agency is doing, how the incident affects the public, and environmental impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure briefings address public concerns and provide context rather than only operational detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Release Basics (Handout 5-3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases are concise dissemination tools—keep them short and formatted correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep to one page; know and use your agency/news release format; know how each media wants to receive releases (fax, email, mail) and follow up with a phone call; have authority to release quotes; be prepared to provide photos; recognize releases may be used to brief officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escort and Media Safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure media safety via escorts and PPE; never allow unescorted media onsite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan in advance to provide protective equipment; coordinate media visits with Operations Section Chief and/or Safety Officer; unescorted media can be unsafe or interfere with operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Aircraft and UAS Coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate any media flights or drone use with Air Operations and follow airspace rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media aircraft may have a right to fly unless FAA has closed the airspace (91.137); if airspace is closed, media need Air Operations Branch Director permission; collect aircraft ID/type/color, proposed entry/exit times, news station name, and passenger names; provide approved radio frequency and discourage unauthorized entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Aircraft Flights and Pooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency-owned or contracted aircraft may be used by media if approved and safe; consider pooling when space is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange flights through Air Operations Branch Director and Incident Commander approval; ensure PPE is available; allow one 'pool' shooter to fly and share images with all organizations; if limited space, consider drawing straws and require winners to share footage.

rubrics_metrics.name: PIOs Should Not Fly Without Approval
rubrics_metrics.description: PIOs must not fly in aircraft unless specifically approved by Air Operations Branch Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow agency safety requirements and approval procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting Media Contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Document media contacts to track communications and issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a communications log or ICS Form 214 for significant events; include caller’s name, news organization, time/date/subject, caller’s phone/email/fax, and whether call was incoming or outgoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring News Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor and archive media coverage for accuracy and documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clip/print newspaper articles and record broadcast stories; order key daily newspapers via Supplies Unit; secure recording devices and appropriate media (e.g., DVD-R) and print/save relevant online coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting the Media with Reporting Tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide resources that help media complete accurate stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer tours, file tape/stock footage, background information (incident summary, facts, correct titles/names), suggested story ideas, briefed interviewees, and regular updates via press releases, fact sheets, photos, videos, briefing packages, and a local web page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Differences with the Media — General
rubrics_metrics.description: Use judgment about when to correct media; avoid allowing differences to distract response efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There will be times to voice concerns and times to remain silent; evaluate whether the situation merits correction and avoid emotional reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Differences with the Media — Internal Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate internally before confronting the media about inaccurate coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk with Public Information staff to identify issues (favoritism, history with media contact); determine whether the problem is the media or incident information operations before contacting the reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Differences with the Media — Remedial Steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing media errors or conflicts, stay professional and seek resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overreact or become defensive; remain calm, courteous, and professional; talk face-to-face with the reporter; offer to clarify information; ask how to prevent recurrence; seek mutual interests; keep Incident Commander and team informed; if unresolved, contact reporter's boss (editor/producer/news director); for serious factual errors in print where corrections are refused, consider drafting a letter to the editor or guest editorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Interview Preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare for interviews by understanding the story and whether you’re the appropriate spokesperson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the reporter about the story type, section/newscast, and expected questions; if unprepared during a phone interview, ask to call back; spokesperson should have in-depth knowledge, a presentable appearance, and a pleasant voice; if not, designate a better spokesperson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Messaging and Concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop and deliver concise key messages; lead with most important facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare two or three key messages; try to get the most important facts in at the beginning; give 20-second answers regardless of medium; anticipate tough questions and rehearse responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Do's and Don'ts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pitfalls in interviews and maintain control of the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not say 'no comment'—explain why you cannot answer if applicable; say 'I can get back to you' if you don't know and then follow through; never guess or speculate; avoid repeating negative or uncomfortable language; when finished answering, be quiet to avoid giving unintended information; do not try to be cute or funny; assume the reporter needs help—use cues like 'The important thing to remember is...' to bridge to your message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality and Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be neutral and represent the agency, not personal opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speak in collective terms (use 'we' rather than 'the Agency thinks'); remember you are an expert managing an incident, not a partisan commentator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Control and Error Handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain composure and correct mistakes responsibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not get angry or argue; if you stumble, ask to start over; remember it's OK to make a mistake—recover by offering to restart or follow up; if you don't know an answer, promise to obtain it and follow through.

rubrics_metrics.name: TV-specific Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare for the visual demands of television interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the background and request changes if inappropriate; wear appropriate, presentable attire (avoid hats and sunglasses unless necessary); look at the reporter rather than the camera; monitor body language, facial expressions, and hand movements; ensure safety equipment and logos are appropriate if on scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficult Interview Techniques (Bridging/Hooking/Flagging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use structured techniques to steer and emphasize messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridging—use key words/phrases to transition to your message; Hooking—include a 'tease' to elicit positive follow-up questions (focus on what's being saved); Flagging—use phrases like 'The main point is...' or 'Remember...' to signal important information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countering Reporter Tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and counter common reporter tactics like loaded questions, false premises, machine-gunning, ambushes, and divide-and-conquer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the tactic (e.g., unacceptable alternatives, hypotheticals, false premises, rapid-fire questions, ambush) and use preparation, bridging, calmness, and offer clarifications or requests for specifics to counter them; consider proactive outreach to reduce ambush risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Reporter Personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt to different reporter types (e.g., Heckler, Interrupter, Twister).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate counter-techniques for each personality and maintain professional composure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live Interview Best Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare for live interviews in the field, studio, or by phone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to interviewer body language; apply difficult-question techniques when needed; be friendly and open; use a backdrop or agency logo to convey responsibility for incident management; wear a uniform or clothing with an agency logo and appropriate safety equipment if in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing Large Numbers of Reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use logistical strategies when many reporters request access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule multiple daily briefings; use videographers/photographers; set up a press room; provide written materials and press kits; designate a spokesperson to centralize communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing Briefings and Press Conferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Set rules and structure to keep briefings orderly and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set and enforce ground rules politely and firmly; begin with a prepared opening statement; have an agenda; take your time with answers; conclude by offering one more question and establish time/place for the next briefing.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Incident Management Is at Fault
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach accountability openly and responsibly when the agency is at fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit mistakes candidly, apologize, explain corrective actions, consider public interest in decisions, respond quickly, involve senior PR expertise in decision-making, and balance legal counsel with the need for credible communication; 'tell the truth—or nothing' is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune’s 14 Corporate PR Principles (Key Points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical crisis PR principles for corporate spokespeople that translate to incident PIO practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights include: make senior leadership responsible for press relations; face facts and admit errors; consider public interest; build relationships with reporters before crises; communicate rather than clam up; respond fast (aim to get your story out within a day in crises); keep lawyers from unduly stalling communications; tell the truth or say nothing; accept that not every story will be perfect; don't take media personally; control what you can (release bad news yourself); know different media and individual reporters; avoid TV unless you can speak candidly in short sound bites; and be human in communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handout 5-2 — Ways to Make Enemies in the Press (Anti-Patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common poor practices that damage media relationships and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: developing overly narrow media lists and ignoring secondary markets; erecting roadblocks and prioritizing editor inquiries to frustrate reporters; returning calls late or with 'no comment'; overreacting to negative coverage by demanding retractions or firing reporters; embargoing or withdrawing advertising from offended media; talking down to reporters; picking and choosing opportunities to cooperate only when immediately beneficial; and other behaviors that erode long-term relationships.
